newsitem.title: GERMANY: Affable Waigel often stuck explaining German mess.
newsitem.headline: Affable Waigel often stuck explaining German mess.

text.p: German politicians who enjoy delivering pithy soundbites when there's good news to tell fall silent and let Finance Minister Theo Waigel do the talking when taxes and debt hit the headlines.
An affable Bavarian, Waigel has a knack for self-deprecating humour to help him now as outrage reigns over his resort to the budgetary sleight-of-hand he had long scorned.

Waigel, 58, married to former German skiing champion Irene Epple and the father of a two-year-old son, is the longest-serving finance minister in the Group of Seven (G7) with more than eight years in the country's least envied job.
But he may also be the most widely derided politician in Germany. Calls for his resignation sound every time budgets go wrong and debt-hating Germans are forced to borrow more money.

Widely respected in international banking circles and an entertaining speaker who fills his addresses with lively anecdotes, Waigel is sometimes called in Germany the "Debt Minister" and the "Finance Chaos Minister".
But he is always good for a laugh.

A favorite story Waigel includes in his speeches is about a group of children who fish him out of a pond. He tries to offer them a reward. While one wants ice cream and another candy, a third child requests asylum.
Waigel: "Why asylum?" The child: "Because if my father found out I saved the finance minister he would kill me."
He jokes that if he ever achieves his plan to cut income tax rates, taxpayers will change their tune to "Theo Gracia," a play on the Latin phrase for "Thanks be to God".

With German deficits surging in recent years, partly because of costly unification with the formerly communist east, joblessness and the high cost of labour, Waigel has been a visible and convenient target for blame.

Hundreds of conservative deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats and Waigel's Christian Social Union on their way into an emergency meeting nervously laughed off requests for comments from a pack of journalists on Thursday.

After the meeting, where deputies were informed about a huge tax shortfall that endangers Germany's chances of qualifying for the single European currency, Kohl slipped away silently by having Waigel divert journalists' attention.

Waigel was -- once again -- left by himself with the thankless task of explaining the new budget holes, the government's controversial plans to tap Bundesbank gold and sell off more shares in Deutsche Telekom.

"Tax increases are never nice," Waigel told reporters. "They have to be well thought out for their effects on the economy. It would be nice if another way can be found with privatisations or other savings.
"But it would be irresponsible of me as finance minister to rule out tax increases with a definite 'no' at this point."
Germany, once the star candidate for membership in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), is desperately trying to rein in its deficit to make sure it qualifies for the euro's launch in 1999.
The Maastricht Treaty says states joining EMU should have budget deficits no higher than three percent of gross domestic product and overall debts not more than 60 percent of GDP.
The crisis erupted on Thursday when a tax commission reported Bonn's expected tax revenues for 1997 would fall 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) short of earlier targets.
That blew a huge hole in Waigel's budget and diminished Germany's chances of qualifying for the euro.
"Why shouldn't we stay relaxed about this?" he responded.
Waigel was born on April 22, 1939, in the Bavarian village of Oberrohr, the son of a bricklayers' foreman. He still commutes to Oberrohr every weekend to his wife and infant son.
Waigel studied law in Munich and Wuerzberg before entering the Bonn parliament in 1972.

From 1976 he was deputy for the Neu-Ulm constituency. He served on the education and science committee, then the committees for budgetary affairs and economics and became finance spokesman for the CDU/CSU after the 1980 election.

After the sudden death of CSU leader Franz-Josef Strauss in 1988, Waigel was elected party chief with 98 per cent of the vote. His hopes of returning to Bavaria were foiled in 1993 when he lost the state premier's race to Edmund Stoiber.
His first marriage to Karin Hoenig in 1966 produced a daughter and son and ended in 1994. A month after the divorce was completed, he married Epple, then 37.
